samples.text:
In some places, big areas of farmland and countryside are now used for solar panels and wind turbines. Some people think this is a good idea, but others disagree. In my opinion, the advantages are more than the disadvantages.

The main advantage is that solar and wind energy are clean. They do not produce carbon dioxide like coal and oil, so they help to reduce global warming and air pollution. Because climate change is a very serious problem for the world, every country need to produce more green energy. Also, the sun and the wind will never finish, so this energy is sustainable for the future. Another advantage is for farmers. They can rent their land to energy companies and receive money every year, which is useful when the farming income is low.

On the other hand, there are some disadvantages. Firstly, when the land is covered with solar panels, it cannot be used for growing food. If many farms do this, the country may need to import more food from other countries. Secondly, many people think that wind turbines are ugly and they destroy the beauty of countryside. Tourists may not want to visit these areas anymore. Also, the building of these projects can damage the habitat of animals and birds, and some birds are killed by the turbines.

In conclusion, using farmland and countryside for solar and wind energy have some negative effects on food production and nature. However, I believe that the fight against climate change are more important, so the advantages outweigh the disadvantages. The government should choose the places careful to reduce the problems.
samples.why: Clear judgement · relevant ideas on both sides but explanation is simple and general · mechanical linking (Firstly, Secondly, Also) · adequate vocabulary, some imprecise · agreement and word-form errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
In a number of regions, extensive areas of farmland and open countryside are being converted into solar farms and wind energy sites. While this raises concerns about food production and the landscape, I believe the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, provided that locations are chosen carefully.

The strongest argument in favour of these projects is the urgent need to reduce carbon emissions. Solar and wind power generate electricity without burning fossil fuels, so expanding them is one of the most effective ways for a country to tackle climate change and improve air quality. Large rural sites are often ideal for this purpose because they receive plenty of sunlight or strong winds and have space for installations that would be impossible in cities. Moreover, these projects can support rural economies. Farmers who lease part of their land to energy companies gain a stable income that does not depend on the weather or crop prices, which can allow them to keep farming the rest of their land.

Nevertheless, there are genuine disadvantages. Covering productive farmland with solar panels reduces the amount of land available for growing food, which could make a country more dependent on imports. Many residents also object to the visual impact of large turbines and rows of panels on landscapes they value, and in some areas this may harm tourism. There are environmental costs as well, since construction can disturb wildlife habitats, and turbines can pose a risk to birds.

However, many of these problems can be reduced. Energy projects can be located on poorer-quality land, and some farms successfully combine solar panels with sheep grazing beneath them.

In conclusion, although using countryside for renewable energy has some impact on agriculture, scenery and wildlife, the need to cut emissions and the economic benefits for rural communities is more pressing. Therefore, I believe the advantages outweigh the disadvantages.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · main ideas extended and supported, with realistic mitigation · clear paragraph focus and varied linking · good collocation (tackle climate change, visual impact) · mostly error-free, one agreement slip.

samples.text:
As countries race to decarbonise their energy systems, farmland and open countryside are increasingly being given over to solar arrays and wind turbines. This has provoked fierce local opposition in some areas, yet I believe that, if sited thoughtfully, such projects deliver benefits that outweigh their costs.

The central argument for these developments is environmental necessity. Replacing coal and gas with renewable electricity is essential if the worst effects of climate change are to be avoided, and generating that electricity at scale requires space that dense urban areas simply cannot provide. Rural sites offer open exposure to sun and wind, relatively low land costs and room for installations large enough to supply thousands of homes. Such projects can also strengthen the rural economy: rental payments from energy companies give farmers a reliable income that cushions them against poor harvests and volatile food prices, while local communities may receive funds for shared facilities.

The objections, however, are not trivial. Agricultural land is a finite resource, and converting large areas of fertile fields to energy generation could undermine a country's capacity to feed itself. Landscapes that have been valued for generations may be transformed by industrial-scale structures, affecting both residents' attachment to their surroundings and the tourism on which some rural areas depend. Poorly planned schemes can also fragment habitats and endanger bird populations.

Crucially, though, most of these drawbacks depend on where and how projects are built rather than on renewable energy itself. Prioritising lower-grade farmland, combining solar panels with grazing, and avoiding sensitive habitats and migration routes can substantially reduce the conflict between energy, food and nature.

In conclusion, the loss of some farmland and scenic value is a genuine cost, but it must be weighed against the far greater threat posed by climate change. With careful planning, the advantages of rural renewable energy projects clearly outweigh the disadvantages.
samples.why: Clear, well-supported judgement · ideas fully extended and logically sequenced · drawbacks evaluated rather than dismissed · wide, precise vocabulary (decarbonise, finite resource, fragment habitats) · wide range of error-free structures.
